stem:
A 9-year-old with facial swelling and noisy breathing is found to have a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray. He is most comfortable sitting upright and becomes cyanosed and distressed when asked to lie flat. The emergency team at a regional hospital is considering CT under sedation.

What is the safest next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Observe locally while arranging a non-urgent outpatient biopsy
options.explanation: Positional cyanosis is an immediate physiological warning, not a reason for outpatient work-up.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep him upright and arrange urgent tertiary retrieval
options.explanation: Maintain the position that best supports breathing and urgently involve retrieval and the specialist team; avoid unplanned sedation or supine positioning.

options.label: C
options.text: Perform an urgent bone marrow aspirate under procedural sedation
options.explanation: An invasive procedure requiring sedation should not precede a safe airway and specialist plan in this setting.

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain a sedated supine CT scan before arranging transfer
options.explanation: Lying flat and sedation can worsen airway or vascular compression; imaging must be planned by a team able to manage that risk.

options.label: E
options.text: Give an oral steroid course and organise outpatient oncology review
options.explanation: Steroids may alter diagnostic tissue and do not replace urgent stabilisation and specialist planning in a child with positional compromise.

context: A symptomatic mediastinal mass can deteriorate with supine positioning, sedation or anaesthesia. Keep the child in the position of comfort and arrange urgent tertiary escalation.
